paras: The attempted lynching of George H. Tew took place on October 12, 1882, at the Aquidneck Park fair near Newport, Rhode Island, when a crowd tried to lynch Tew, a young special officer, after he struck a boy with his club. Tew escaped to a neighboring farmhouse, where regular officers protected him, and the next day he was charged with beating the boy. Papers across the country carried the story as a near-lynching of a policeman, and most of them blamed the officer.

Tew was serving as a special officer at the races held during the Aquidneck fair. According to the New York Sun's Newport dispatch, a boy had run across the track, and Tew felled him with his club. A wire note printed in the Evening Critic and the Daily Dispatch called it an "unprovoked attack on a boy with a club."

The Sun reported that onlookers who saw the child "writhing" raised the cry "Kill the villain" and rushed at the officer. Men on horseback broke through the crowd to him, and Tew then ran for his life and took refuge in a farmhouse. The crowd surrounded the house, demanded that he surrender and threatened to break down the doors, while the farmer came out armed to defend his home.

Regular officers arrived and protected Tew from the crowd, and the Sun said a posse of officers rescued him and took him into town to be prosecuted. No injury to Tew is reported, and the reports give no race for him, the boy or the crowd.

On October 13 the officer, named in a Newport court dispatch as Wm. H. Tew, was brought to court, pleaded not guilty and was sent to jail to await trial the following Tuesday. No report of the trial or its outcome, or of any action against members of the crowd, was found.

The story ran as a Newport dispatch the next day, under headlines such as "Nearly a Lynching" in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and "Attempt to Lynch a Policeman" in the New York Sun. The Sun gave the fullest account, called the blow an "outrage" and described Tew as a disciple of a New York police captain. The Omaha Daily Bee printed the same short dispatch as Wheeling on October 14, and the Portland Daily Press followed the case into court.

A syndicated weekly news column carried the story into small papers from Kansas to Mississippi later in October, remarking that Tew "thought it part of his duty as a special policeman to use his club on a boy." Throughout, the coverage cast the officer rather than the crowd as the wrongdoer and did not condemn the attempt to lynch him.
Papers differ on the officer's name: most give George H. Tew, the weekly brief gives G. H. Tew, and the Newport court dispatch of October 13 gives Wm. H. Tew.

bases: Every report describes a crowd's attempt to lynch a special officer who had clubbed a boy; he escaped to a farmhouse and was protected by police, and no one was killed (A1, A2, A3).

A crowd, described as a 'mob', tried to lynch Tew to punish his alleged clubbing of a boy, but he reached a farmhouse and officers protected him, so no one was killed; it was an attempted lynching (A1, A3, A5).

Separate dispatches in the Sun, the Wheeling/Omaha wire report, the Evening Critic news note and the Portland court dispatch agree on the clubbing, the crowd's attempt and the officers' protection (A1, A2, A3, A5).

framing.detail: The coverage condemned the officer rather than the crowd: 'unprovoked attack', 'outrage', 'Too Much Brute Force' (Omaha headline as OCR'd), and the ironic 'thought it part of his duty'.
Most papers ran the short wire note in news-brief columns without comment.

conflicts.note: All refer to the same fair incident; the Portland court dispatch is a separate, later report but stands alone against the others on the first name.

versions.value: The boy had run across the track before Tew struck him

conflicts.note: The Sun gives a reason the officer acted but still calls the blow an outrage; the versions differ in detail more than in judgment.
